data.title: Crown Crafts (NASDAQ:CRWS) Is Posting Promising Earnings But The Good News Doesn’t Stop There
data.description:
Crown Crafts, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:CRWS) solid earnings announcement recently didn't do much to the stock price. We did some analysis to find out why and believe that investors might be missing some encouraging factors contained in the earnings.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

A Closer Look At Crown Crafts' Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Crown Crafts has an accrual ratio of -0.18 for the year to September 2026. That implies it has very good cash conversion, and that its earnings in the last year actually significantly understate its free cash flow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$14m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$5.17m. Crown Crafts' free cash flow improved over the last year, which is generally good to see.

data.title: There May Be Reason For Hope In MT Højgaard Holding's (CPH:MTHH) Disappointing Earnings
data.description:
The market was pleased with the recent earnings report from MT Højgaard Holding A/S (CPH:MTHH), despite the profit numbers being soft. Our analysis suggests that investors may have noticed some promising signs beyond the statutory profit figures.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Examining Cashflow Against MT Højgaard Holding's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, MT Højgaard Holding recorded an accrual ratio of -0.14. That implies it has good cash conversion, and implies that its free cash flow solidly exceeded its profit last year. To wit, it produced free cash flow of kr.238m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of kr.152.5m. MT Højgaard Holding's free cash flow actually declined over the last year, which is disappointing, like non-biodegradable balloons.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On MT Højgaard Holding's Profit Performance

As we discussed above, MT Højgaard Holding has perfectly satisfactory free cash flow relative to profit. Because of this, we think MT Højgaard Holding's earnings potential is at least as good as it seems, and maybe even better! Unfortunately, though, its earnings per share actually fell back over the last year. Of course, we've only just scratched the surface when it comes to analysing its earnings; one could also consider margins, forecast growth, and return on investment, among other factors. So if you'd like to dive deeper into this stock, it's crucial to consider any risks it's facing. Case in point: We've spotted 2 warning signs for MT Højgaard Holding you should be aware of.

data.title: 3 Funds With Capital Market Exposure After Anthropic’s Record IPO
data.description:
Two funds both tied to capital markets can look similar on paper, yet one like IAI can be almost 100% in investment banks and exchanges, while another like IYF has less than a third there and far more in broader financials. That split matters when a company like Anthropic lists in a record US$81.3b IPO and pushes large underwriting and trading volumes through the system. Those flows feed directly into the businesses that run the deals and platforms. Investors looking to explore that angle can consider how IAI, KCE and IYF provide three distinct ETF approaches to this area of the market.

Where could strong businesses be hiding behind a cheap share price? Explore 35 high quality undervalued stocks combining solid balance sheets and cash flows with potential value beyond the headline.

iShares U.S. Broker-Dealers & Securities Exchanges ETF (IAI)

Holdings: 40 | In capital markets: 99.8% of the fund

Goldman Sachs at 17.76% is a large Wall Street investment bank that helps run IPO books, so a jumbo deal like the Anthropic listing can mean more advisory and underwriting revenue flowing through a major slice of IAI. Morgan Stanley at 15.07% also leans on capital markets work, while Charles Schwab at 8.55% is closer to retail brokerage and trading volumes. Together, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley make up 32.8% of this ETF. This gives you a concentrated tilt toward investment banking and brokerage, alongside exchanges and data groups that sit on 40.2% of the portfolio by industry weight.

You are effectively betting that investment banks and trading platforms keep finding enough deal flow and turnover to justify such a focused approach, with 99.8% of the fund in capital markets businesses. Simply Wall St's fair value work suggests 56.1% of IAI by weight is in holdings trading below its estimates of fair value. Some investors may see this as a reason to research this ETF further. Heavy reliance on a handful of big brokers and dealers is the flip side, because any sector wide slump in underwriting or trading activity would hit a large portion of your exposure at once.

Not every stock inside IAI is priced the same way. Find out how many of IAI's holdings look undervalued.

State Street SPDR S&P Capital Markets ETF (KCE)

Holdings: 68 | In capital markets: 99.8% of the fund

This ETF gives you a broad mix of capital markets businesses that can all touch an Anthropic sized IPO in different ways. Asset managers and custody banks make up 45.4% of the portfolio, with another 29.0% in investment banking and brokerage and 25.4% in exchanges and data. Donnelley Financial Solutions and Tradeweb Markets together are 4.3% of the fund, while Cboe Global Markets adds listed trading infrastructure that can see more activity when a high profile new listing starts trading. About 34% of KCE overlaps with IAI, so much of the rest is in capital markets companies IAI does not hold.

The ETF relies on the S&P Capital Markets Select Industry Index to keep the focus on capital markets, and on a spread of 68 holdings where Simply Wall St estimates that 45.2% of the fund by weight sits below its fair value estimates. That design makes KCE a closer call if you want the theme but do not want a small group of brokers dominating your exposure. Donnelley Financial Solutions carries more of the fund than Tradeweb Markets, which still leaves neither company anywhere near a controlling weight.

Uncover whether KCE has kept pace with the market over the past week, year and five years

iShares U.S. Financials ETF (IYF)

Holdings: 147 | In capital markets: 32.4% of the fund

This ETF gives you a capital markets link through Berkshire Hathaway at 13.04% and JPMorgan Chase at 10.93%, which together are a heavy 24.0% of the fund. Both can benefit if an Anthropic scale IPO feeds more underwriting revenue, trading activity and related banking work into their broader franchises. Only 32.4% of the portfolio is in capital markets industries, with the rest spread across diversified banks, insurance groups and other financials, so the direct effect of a single listing is cushioned by plenty of businesses tied to lending, premiums and fee income.

Simply Wall St estimates that 84.1% of this ETF by weight is in holdings trading below its assessment of fair value. This may interest investors who want the capital markets angle without giving up wider financials exposure. That mix leaves you leaning on a big pair of banks and a broad set of insurers, asset managers and exchanges to share the load, but it also means Anthropic related activity is only one of several forces likely to drive the fund over time.

Ten companies make up 48.5% of IYF. Find out which ones, and how much each carries.

The exposure trade-off

If you want the Anthropic IPO front and centre, IAI and KCE are the closest fit. Both keep 99.8% of assets in capital markets industries, where underwriting fees, trading commissions and index adjustments from a US$81b listing flow first. IAI leans hardest on a few large banks and exchanges, with Goldman Sachs alone carrying the highest single weight of the trio. KCE spreads that same theme over more holdings, so Donnelley Financial Solutions, Tradeweb Markets and others each play a smaller part. Underwriters and trading platforms need to keep a strong grip on allocations and aftermarket activity for this to matter.

IYF turns the dial down. Only 32.4% of the fund sits in capital markets, with the rest in broader banking and insurance. Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase connect you to Anthropic related activity, yet much of the ETF is driven by lending, balance sheet strength and insurance premiums instead. IAI has the highest share of holdings below Simply Wall St fair value estimates, KCE the lowest and IYF the highest of all three. Costs cluster between US$35 and US$37 a year on a US$10,000 holding, and five year returns landed within 1.5 percentage points of one another. Your call is which mix of concentration, capital markets weight and broader financials suits what you want from this news.

With 17.76% of IAI riding on Goldman Sachs Group, its next few years matter as much as the fund's. See the earnings forecasts for Goldman Sachs Group.

data.title: 3 ETFs For AMD After Its OpenAI News গল্প
data.description:
You might like Advanced Micro Devices for its chips and artificial intelligence work, but holding the stock on its own means living with its specific risks. Simply Wall St flags a volatile share price over the past 3 months compared to the US market, and also significant insider selling over the same period. Owning AMD inside an exchange traded fund spreads those company issues across many holdings, which also spreads out any future gains from AMD itself.

Right now the story has a fresh twist. OpenAI president Greg Brockman says OpenAI’s models helped AMD squeeze roughly an extra year of chip progress into less than five months, and the upgrades are already baked into a design that is ready for manufacturing. With that backdrop, you might look at SMH, XLK and SOXX as ways to hold AMD through a broader portfolio.

Prefer to pick the companies yourself? Start with 53 AI infrastructure stocks.

VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH)

SMH is heavily built around chip producers, with 77.3% in semiconductors and another 17.9% in semiconductor materials and equipment. Advanced Micro Devices is a meaningful slice at 6.45%, so roughly US$64 of every US$1,000 goes into AMD. NVIDIA and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing are even larger positions and anchor the fund’s exposure to different parts of the chip supply chain. A small allocation to application software at 4.6% adds a different revenue stream beside hardware focused groups.

AMD’s share price has been more volatile than the broader US market over the past three months, and that affects your position in SMH as well. Other chip holdings such as NVIDIA move with many of the same industry drivers, so the fund mostly spreads that volatility across peers rather than cancelling it out. You still end up relying on one sector’s mood remaining supportive of semiconductor stocks trading at higher prices.

An ETF's price is just the sum of what it holds. Check whether SMH trades above or below its holdings' estimated cash flow value.

State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK)

Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA pull XLK toward large US technology platforms, with semiconductors at 35.9% and big slices in hardware, software and communications equipment alongside them. That mix means Advanced Micro Devices is important but not dominant. At 5.43% of the portfolio and the number 5 position, each US$1,000 in XLK puts about US$54 into Advanced Micro Devices while spreading the rest across 78 other holdings. About 42% of XLK overlaps SMH, yet the heavier stakes in broad software and hardware groups provide exposure that SMH does not.

Significant insider selling at Advanced Micro Devices over the past 3 months may worry investors who only hold the individual stock. XLK cannot change what insiders do at the company, although it does tie that risk to businesses whose fortunes depend more on consumer devices, cloud services or enterprise software than on the same chips. Investors gain a blend of semiconductors, hardware, software and communications equipment that is not available from Advanced Micro Devices on its own.

See how XLK's returns compare with the market, from one week to five years

iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX)

SOXX gives Advanced Micro Devices a central role, with 10.86% of the portfolio and roughly US$109 of every US$1,000 you invest tied to the stock. That is a real slice of what you would own. The rest closely resembles SMH, with 83.7% in semiconductor companies and 16.4% in semiconductor materials and equipment. Broadcom and Micron Technology join Advanced Micro Devices near the top, and together those leading positions concentrate your money in a tight group of chip specialists.

There is a risk that Advanced Micro Devices sees revenue growth and earnings from higher value products capped if demand or pricing does not support them. SOXX only partly softens that issue because Broadcom, Micron and many peers still depend on the same broad semiconductor cycle in different segments. This keeps your exposure tied to chip makers even as it is spread across several balance sheets, and it leaves industry wide swings firmly in play.

See what you'd actually own if you bought SOXX, from its 34 positions to how much sits in the top 10.

Choosing your Advanced Micro Devices fund exposure

If you want AMD front and center after the recent AI design news, SOXX is the most concentrated option. Around US$109 of every US$1,000 tracks Advanced Micro Devices, and the rest stays in a tight group of chip and chip equipment businesses. That focus cuts two ways if revenue from higher value products does not meet the expectations set in the current share price.

If you prefer to keep AMD meaningful but not dominant while paying less each year, SMH puts roughly US$64 of every US$1,000 into the stock, while XLK sits closer to US$54 and holds almost three times as many companies as SMH. XLK also carries the lowest fee at about US$8 annually on US$10,000. Your choice is between a heavier semiconductor tilt with SMH, a broader technology mix with XLK, or the most concentrated AMD exposure with SOXX.

Owning SMH means owning a sizeable slice of NVIDIA. Find out the risks our analysis flags for NVIDIA.
